title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
authors: Andi Gu, Alek H. Kemeny, Susanne F. Yelin, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.
summary: This paper presents a novel, AI-driven framework where Large Language Models co-design quantum circuits for complex problems. By integrating LLM proposal generation with an independent quantum circuit evaluator, the authors significantly optimized resource usage for tasks ranging from number theory to quantum simulation. This work opens a new avenue for algorithm discovery in quantum computation.
main_problem: Developing efficient, reversible quantum algorithms for complex tasks like arithmetic, decoding, and simulation, while overcoming the constraints of quantum computation.
main_result: The authors introduced an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that successfully discovered quantum circuits significantly reducing resource costs (Toffoli gates and qubits) across diverse computational tasks.
method: They employed an evolutionary framework where Large Language Models propose circuit designs, which are then verified and scored by an independent evaluator, allowing for high-level structural revisions.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum circuits designed to perform reversible computations, specifically addressing the constraints of reversibility and coherent control flow in quantum information processing.
key_observables: Toffoli count (T), peak qubit count (Q), and the combined TQ-cost, used to benchmark circuit efficiency against state-of-the-art methods.
important_parameters: The complexity of the task (e.g., modular inversion, Reed-Solomon decoding) and the resource budget (T and Q).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that LLMs can propose novel, structurally sound circuit candidates that go beyond simple equivalence-preserving rewrites.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the discovery pipeline, showing how LLMs propose and the evaluator refines circuits for tasks like conditional routing and decoding computational history.
paper_structure: The paper details the general LLM-guided optimization framework, followed by specific applications demonstrating improvements in Reed-Solomon decoding, modular inversion, and lattice gauge theory calculations.
why_interesting: The methodology of using generative AI (LLMs) to guide the discovery of novel, resource-efficient quantum algorithms is a major development for quantum computing theory.

The LLM proposes architecturally different approaches (algorithm families; here extended Euclidean, Berlekamp–Massey, and Peterson–Gorenstein–Zierler (PGZ) decoders), which are then developed and optimized in parallel. Strong candidates are periodically shared between families to allow for cross-pollination of useful ideas. FIG. 3 Making divsteps reversible with minimal overhead. (a) Excursion depth j in one representative walk. Dots mark ambiguous decisions. We use a cutoff jstore = 5, so all ambiguous decisions with j ≥5 are stored rather than decoded. The histogram shows the distribution of excursion depths over uniformly sampled walks: only 12.4% of ambiguous decisions reach j ≥5. (b) Empirical stopping-time and history-size distributions. The discovered circuit assumes that every walk terminates between steps 499 and 533; this assumption fails with probability ∼10−5. It also allocates enough qubits to store at most 60 branch decisions, which is sufficient for all but a 2.4 × 10−6 fraction of walks.
